Baby & Child

Swollen lymph nodes in children: what to notice and when to get help

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A small lump in your child’s neck or beneath the ear can be unsettling. Often it is a lymph node responding to a nearby infection. Most childhood lymph-node swelling has a reassuring explanation, but the child’s general health, changes in the lump and any difficulty breathing or swallowing matter more than the location alone.

Why lymph nodes become noticeable

Lymph nodes are small structures containing immune cells. They are found throughout the body, including the neck, armpits and groin, and help the immune system respond to germs. They are often called glands in everyday conversation, although lymph nodes and saliva-producing glands are different structures.

When a child has a cold, sore throat or another viral or bacterial infection, nearby nodes may enlarge as part of the immune response. Fever may accompany the illness, but fever itself is not the cause of a swollen node. Some small nodes can also be felt in children who are otherwise well.

Inflammation in an area of the body can activate the nodes that drain it. An enlarged node therefore does not automatically mean that the node itself is infected, that antibiotics are needed or that a serious disease is present.

Skin inflammation, eczema and lumps below the ear

A scrape, cut, burn or insect bite may become inflamed or provide an entry point for a skin infection. Nearby lymph nodes can then become more noticeable. For example, an infected finger or arm may be accompanied by a tender node in the armpit.

Children with persistent eczema on the head or neck can have prominent nearby nodes. Inflamed skin can also become infected, but enlargement alone does not prove that bacteria are entering the body or that the eczema needs antibiotics. Spreading redness, warmth, pain, discharge or fever should be assessed.

Swelling beneath or behind an ear is not always a lymph node. Mumps, for example, usually causes swelling of the parotid salivary glands around the cheek and jaw. It can be mistaken for swollen neck nodes, so a clinician may need to examine the area.

Cancer is an uncommon explanation for enlarged nodes in children. It remains one of the possibilities considered when a lump persists, grows or is accompanied by concerning symptoms. Mentioning that possibility is a reason for appropriate follow-up, not a prediction about a particular child.

What you may see or feel

One node, a group of nodes or nodes in several parts of the body may enlarge. Tender lumps in the neck can accompany tonsillitis or another throat infection. Nodes elsewhere may react to an infection in the area they drain.

A node may be sore when touched, and an infected node may have warm or red skin over it. Some reactive nodes are painless. Enlarged nodes can occasionally become several centimetres across, but a large or growing lump should be examined rather than assumed to be an ordinary cold-related change.

Nodes may remain noticeable for weeks or even months after an infection, and small normal nodes can remain palpable. Duration alone does not identify the cause. An already-assessed reactive node in a well child differs from a new unexplained lump. Follow the agreed review plan and seek advice if a new swelling is not starting to get smaller after about a week, or sooner if it grows or other symptoms appear.

When to seek help promptly

Get emergency help if neck swelling causes breathing difficulty, or if your child is struggling to swallow saliva, drooling with distress or becoming severely unwell. These are not symptoms to leave for a routine appointment.

Seek prompt medical advice for a rapidly enlarging lump, red or very painful skin over a node, fever with significant swelling, restricted neck movement, difficulty drinking or a child who looks unusually ill. A young infant with fever or an unexplained lump needs early medical assessment.

Arrange a review if there is no clear recent infection, if a node remains enlarged without improving, if it feels unusually firm or fixed, or if nodes are enlarged in several body regions. A lump just above or below the collarbone also needs medical assessment. Unexplained weight loss, night sweats or unusual bruising deserve attention.

Size is one part of the assessment. A clearly large node, especially one measured around 2.5 cm or more, warrants prompt advice, but do not wait for a lump to reach a specific size when other warning signs are present. A comparison such as “bigger than a marble” is too variable to decide whether care is needed.

Persistent fever with swollen neck nodes, a rash, red eyes, cracked or red lips, a red tongue, or red and swollen hands and feet can be a sign of Kawasaki disease. This uncommon condition needs urgent assessment because it can affect the heart. Do not wait for every feature to appear or for a particular number of fever days if your child is unwell.

What the clinician may check

The clinician may ask when the lump appeared, how it has changed and whether your child has had a sore throat, dental problem, skin infection or recent illness. Other symptoms and the presence of lumps elsewhere are relevant.

Examination helps distinguish a lymph node from another type of swelling and identify a possible source of infection. The clinician may check the ears, throat, mouth, skin and other node groups.

A well child with a typical reactive node may only need observation and a follow-up plan. Blood tests, ultrasound or other investigations are selected when the findings need explanation or an abscess is suspected. Not every swollen node requires a scan or biopsy.

Treatment depends on the cause

Care follows the cause. For a viral illness, treatment usually focuses on comfort, fluids and relief of troublesome symptoms while the immune system deals with the infection. Antibiotics do not treat the virus or make every reactive node disappear.

If a bacterial infection is suspected or confirmed, the clinician may prescribe an antibiotic suitable for the child and the likely infection. Follow the prescribed directions and return for reassessment if the child worsens or does not improve as expected.

Sometimes the node itself becomes infected, called lymphadenitis. It can be enlarged, very tender and covered by red skin. A collection of pus, or abscess, may develop. This needs prompt assessment and may require antibiotics, hospital treatment or drainage by a clinical team.

Drainage is not needed for every enlarged node, and the appropriate procedure depends on the cause. Never squeeze, puncture or try to drain a lump at home.

Looking after your child and following up

Offer drinks and rest, and ask a pharmacist or clinician about an age-appropriate pain or fever medicine if your child is uncomfortable. Follow the product and clinical instructions rather than choosing a dose from an adult medicine supply. A baby younger than three months with fever needs urgent medical assessment; do not delay assessment to try fever medicine.

Avoid repeatedly pressing the lump to check it. Note when it appeared, associated symptoms and any obvious change, and follow the review interval agreed with the clinician. The aim is to notice a meaningful change without continually irritating the area.

A node does not have to vanish the moment a cold ends. Seek another review if it grows, new symptoms appear, your child seems less well or the swelling is not following the expected course. A reassuring first examination should still include advice about when to come back.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Most childhood neck-node enlargement follows infection, and a well child may only need observation.

A red, very tender or rapidly growing node needs assessment; breathing difficulty needs emergency help.

Antibiotics and drainage are used for specific bacterial problems, not for every swollen gland.

Persistent fever with Kawasaki features needs urgent assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note when swelling started, related symptoms and the follow-up advice you receive. A record can support a clinical conversation, but it cannot identify a lump or determine whether an antibiotic is needed.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for breathing difficulty or severe swallowing difficulty with distress. Get prompt advice for a rapidly growing, red or very painful lump, a feverish young infant or a child who appears very ill. This article is educational and cannot diagnose a lump or replace individual medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Many swollen nodes reflect a normal immune response to infection.
  • Eczema-related nodes do not automatically mean bacterial infection.
  • Mumps usually affects salivary glands, which are different from lymph nodes.
  • Changes in the lump and the child’s overall condition guide follow-up.
  • Do not squeeze or attempt to drain a swollen node.

Frequently asked questions

Is a swollen gland beneath my child’s ear dangerous?

Often it reflects a nearby infection and settles over time. However, not every swelling in that area is a lymph node. Have an unexplained, enlarging or painful lump assessed, and seek emergency help if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult.

Can eczema cause swollen lymph nodes?

Persistent eczema, especially on the head and neck, can make nearby nodes prominent. Skin infection is also possible, but a swollen node alone does not prove infection or a need for antibiotics.

What symptoms can swollen nodes cause?

You may notice a lump in the neck, armpit or another area. It may be tender, and an infected node can have warm or red skin over it. The symptoms of the underlying illness, such as a sore throat or fever, may be more noticeable than the node itself.

When should I take my child to the doctor?

Seek advice for unexplained or persistent swelling, significant enlargement, increasing pain, redness or a child who seems unwell. Breathing difficulty, severe swallowing problems or rapid deterioration need urgent or emergency care rather than a routine appointment.

Does a swollen lymph node always need antibiotics?

No. Viral infections and other reactive changes usually do not benefit from antibiotics. A clinician decides whether there is a bacterial infection that needs treatment.

Why is the lump still there after the cold has gone?

Reactive nodes can take weeks or months to become smaller, and small normal nodes may remain palpable. Follow the agreed review plan. A new unexplained lump, or one not starting to shrink after about a week, should be discussed with a clinician; return sooner if it grows, becomes red or painful, or your child develops other symptoms.

Is mumps the same as swollen lymph nodes?

No. Mumps typically inflames salivary glands near the ears and jaw. Because the swellings can look similar, examination may be needed to identify what is enlarged.

Can I massage or squeeze the node to make it smaller?

No. Repeated pressure can irritate the area, and trying to drain it can cause injury or infection. A suspected abscess needs assessment and treatment by a clinical team.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
